  Code                    APM_51055_EP
  Team and workload       Course coordinator: Rémi Flamary (École Polytechnique, CMAP) · instructors: Mansour Benbakoura · 36 h in person (lecture/tutorial/lab split not published on the sheet) · 4.5 ECTS (value retained for the LLGA; 5 ECTS for the École Polytechnique degree and exchange programs, 4 ECTS for the MScT Artificial Intelligence and Advanced Visual Computing) · teaching languages: French and English ("in English or in French depending on the audience, with course materials in English") · signals, Fourier, sampling, filtering, time-frequency analysis, spectral estimation — up to the spectrograms consumed by ML and the spectral distances of optimal transport (the same instructor's M1P2 module).

  ----------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: an engineer who consumes audio / series / images in ML and wants the chain before the network. **Empirical first**: an unreadable spectrogram from a bad window; aliasing that invents a frequency — then we name LTI, Fourier, Shannon, STFT.

Bridge to speech, spectral OT, sensors: the raw material of modern AI.

### What you will be able to do

-   Characterize a signal and a linear time-invariant system (impulse, frequency response, stability, causality).
-   Move from time to frequency with confidence: Fourier series, Fourier transform, and a reasoned choice of representation.
-   Apply the Shannon theorem and understand what "sampling well" requires — and what aliasing is.
-   Implement a DFT/FFT and design digital low-pass, high-pass, band-pass filters.
-   Analyze a non-stationary signal through time-frequency analysis and wavelets rather than the global transform alone.
-   Estimate the spectrum of a random signal (periodogram, averaging) and interpret its noise.
-   Connect spectral representation and learning: why a spectrogram is a good input for a neural network.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026-2027 catalog)

**Official objectives** (paraphrased from the description published on SynapseS): historically driven by telecommunications, signal processing is today present in every field that analyzes, extracts and transforms digital information. The course introduces the field — Fourier analysis and analog filtering (with modulation and Fourier optics as examples), sampling and digital filtering which have become the standard of applications, the fast Fourier transform algorithm, image filtering, then the *random* aspects of signals and the optimal linear filtering of the signal/noise pair modeled as a stochastic process (autoregressive models, Wiener filtering). It concludes with the common representations of signals — the discrete cosine transform and wavelets (JPEG encoding, image reconstruction), the short-time Fourier transform for non-stationary signals — and with recent approaches coming from machine learning: learned dictionaries and signal reconstruction by deep learning. All of it is complemented by **Python/NumPy labs** (generating an audio signal, filtering). **Official assessment: lab reports (40%) and a final theoretical and practical written exam (60%).**

### Where this course fits in the program

Recommended option of the LLGA track in Year 1 · Period 1 (36 h, 4.5 ECTS). The official prerequisites of the description — basic knowledge of *analysis* (Fourier transform), *probability* (random variables and processes) and *linear algebra*, plus Python/NumPy for the labs — correspond exactly to the foundations of the two refresher modules: [Refresher in Statistics](../m1p1-refresher-statistics/index.html) for the probability theory useful for random signals, and [Refresher in Computer Science](../m1p1-refresher-cs/index.html) for NumPy and the implementation of the labs; the review chapter (ch. 0) moreover takes up Fourier theory at the required level. The course unit is shared with the engineering cycle (X), the DAIIG and MJH master's programs and the other MScT tracks (AI&AVC, ViCAI, TRAI).

Downstream, three modules directly consume this course. [Speech Technology for Conversational AI](../m2-speech-technology/index.html) (M2) starts from the speech signal representations introduced here; [Multimodal Generative AI](../m1p2-multimodal-genai/index.html) leverages spectrograms as the interface between audio and models; [Computational Optimal Transport for ML and Fairness](../m1p2-optimal-transport/index.html), a module by the same instructor, uses the spectral distances (sinkhorn on spectrograms) whose foundations are laid in the chapter "The signal for modern ML". The course also sheds light on the filtering and convolution that [Image Analysis and Computer Vision](../m1p1-computer-vision/index.html) mobilizes from its first chapters.

### Course outline

-   **Review: Fourier series in the L² sense, Fubini**: the functional analysis tools from which the whole course follows.
-   **Signals and linear systems**: impulse response, convolution, stability — the common framework.
-   **The Fourier series**: decomposing a periodic signal, in the L² sense and beyond intuition.
-   **The Fourier transform**: the universal time-frequency change of variable and its properties.
-   **Sampling: the Shannon theorem**: from the continuous to the discrete without losing information — or knowing that you are.
-   **DFT, FFT and digital filtering**: the discrete transform, its fast algorithm, and filter design.
-   **Time-frequency analysis and wavelets**: representing a signal whose content evolves — the short-time Fourier window and beyond.
-   **Random signals and spectral estimation**: noise, periodogram, estimating the spectrum of a process.
-   **The signal for modern ML**: spectrograms as network inputs, spectral losses — the explicit bridge to learning.
-   **The teacher's research: from signals to optimal transport**: Rémi Flamary's research, from signal matching to regularized optimal transport.

### How to study this module

-   Work through the review chapter even if you come from an applied background: the Fourier series in the L² sense is presented there with exactly the level required afterwards.
-   Listen to your transforms: every lab can be validated by ear (filtered sound, sampled sound) — perceptual checking is an excellent error detector.
-   Redo in NumPy an FFT and a filtering on a real signal (audio, sensor) before using the ready-made functions.
-   Memorize the properties of the Fourier transform (duality, convolution-product): they save half the computations of the exercises.
-   Spend time on random signals, often new to students: they are the key to spectral estimation and to the M2 audio modules.
-   Finish with the chapter "The signal for modern ML" then with the teacher's research: this is the best preparation for [Computational Optimal Transport](../m1p2-optimal-transport/index.html) and [Speech Technology](../m2-speech-technology/index.html).

::: note
[Note Extrapolons]{.tag} The conversational and generative models at the heart of the LLGA master's program consume signals: speech, music, sensors. This module provides the spectral culture shared by the engineers who will deploy these systems and the researchers who will invent their representations — from the spectrogram to transport distances.
:::

## 0. Review: Fourier series in the L² sense, Fubini {#ch0}

:::: recap
::: recap-title
L3 background used
:::

-   **The Hilbert space $L^2$**: hermitian inner product $\langle f, g\rangle = \int f(t)\,\overline{g(t)}\,dt$, Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, orthogonal projection onto a finite-dimensional subspace — Fourier = a change of basis in an *infinite orthonormal* basis;
-   **Fubini's theorem**: if $\iint \|f(x,y)\|\,dx\,dy < \infty$ (or for positive functions), the order of integration is free — it justifies all the convolution computations of chapter 3;
-   **Integration by parts** and changes of variable;
-   **Complex geometric sequences**, which give the orthogonality of the exponentials.
::::

::: prop
[Proposition 0.1 — The exponentials form an orthogonal system]{.tag} On $[0, T_0]$, set $e_k(t) = e^{ik\omega_0 t}$ with $\omega_0 = 2\pi/T_0$. Then $$\langle e_k, e_\ell\rangle = \int_0^{T_0} e^{i(k-\ell)\omega_0 t}\,dt = \begin{cases} T_0 & \text{if } k = \ell,\\[2pt] \dfrac{e^{i(k-\ell)\omega_0 T_0} - 1}{i(k-\ell)\omega_0} = 0 & \text{if } k \neq \ell,\end{cases}$$ since $e^{i(k-\ell)\omega_0 T_0} = e^{2i\pi(k-\ell)} = 1$. The $e_k / \sqrt{T_0}$ therefore form an orthonormal system of $L^2([0,T_0])$.
:::

::: def
[Definition 0.2 — The Dirichlet and Fejér kernels]{.tag} The **partial sum** of order $N$ of a Fourier series can be written as a convolution with the **Dirichlet kernel** $$D_N(\theta) = \sum_{k=-N}^{N} e^{ik\theta} = \frac{\sin\big((N+\tfrac12)\theta\big)}{\sin(\theta/2)},$$ while the Cesàro mean of the partial sums (arithmetic mean $S_0, \dots, S_{N-1}$) is written with the **Fejér kernel** $F_N = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n<N} D_n$, which has the decisive property of being **positive** ($F_N \geq 0$) and of mass 1.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 0.3 — Fejér convergence, density, completeness]{.tag}

-   **Fejér**: for $f$ continuous and $T_0$-periodic, $\sigma_N f = f \* F_N \to f$ *uniformly*. The proof uses $F_N \geq 0$, $\int F_N = 1$ and the concentration of the mass of $F_N$ near 0.
-   **Consequence (density)**: the trigonometric polynomials $\sum_{\|k\| \leq N} c_k e^{ik\omega_0 t}$ are dense in $L^2([0,T_0])$.
-   **Consequence (Hilbert basis)**: the orthonormal system $\{e_k/\sqrt{T_0}\}$ is *complete*: it is a Hilbert basis of $L^2$. The whole theory of Fourier series "in the $L^2$ sense" follows from it.
:::

::: note
[Dirichlet versus Fejér — the message to remember]{.tag} The partial sums themselves (Dirichlet kernel, which changes sign) do not converge uniformly for every continuous function: they "oscillate" near discontinuities (Gibbs phenomenon, quantified in ch. 2). The Cesàro average smooths these oscillations. Moral: *in $L^2$, everything converges nicely; uniformly, one must regularize (averaging, windows) — exactly the role of the Hann windows of ch. 5.*
:::

## 1. Signals and linear systems {#ch1}

Concrete scene: a fine-tuned speech model that drops because Mel was poorly parameterized upstream. This chapter fixes signal and LTI.

::: note
[What breaks]{.tag} Undersampling below Nyquist; too short a window (resolution); treating filtering as an ML black box.
:::

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Signal, LTI system]{.tag} A **signal** is a function $x : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ (or $\mathbb{C}$), or a sequence $x : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{R}$ (discrete signal). A **system** transforms one signal into another; it is *LTI* (linear time-invariant) if $x \mapsto y = T(x)$ satisfies: linearity, and $x(\cdot - \tau) \mapsto y(\cdot - \tau)$ for every delay $\tau$. We write $\delta_\tau$ for the Dirac mass at $\tau$ (discrete: $\delta_{n}$ = the sequence equal to 1 at $n$, 0 elsewhere).
:::

:::: thm
[Proposition 1.2 — Convolution representation (proved)]{.tag} Every LTI system (discrete, and continuous subject to a continuity condition) is entirely described by its **impulse response** $h = T(\delta_0)$: $$y(t) = (x \* h)(t) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} x(\tau)\, h(t - \tau)\, d\tau \qquad \Big(\text{discrete: } y[n] = \sum_k x[k]\,h[n-k]\Big).$$

::: proof
Discrete version (the continuous argument replaces the sums by integrals against Dirac masses, $x = \int x(\tau)\,\delta_\tau\,d\tau$, which requires a minimum of distribution theory — admitted here). In discrete time, $x = \sum_k x[k]\,\delta_k$ (a sum of "column" sequences). By linearity, $T(x) = \sum_k x[k]\,T(\delta_k)$. By invariance, $T(\delta_k) = \tau_k h$, where $(\tau_k h)[n] = h[n-k]$. Hence $y[n] = \sum_k x[k]\,h[n-k]$. Commutativity follows from the change of variable $\tau' = t - \tau$ (Fubini: the integral is absolutely convergent under the stability assumptions below).[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.3 — BIBO stability and causality (proved)]{.tag} The LTI system with impulse response $h$ is:

-   **BIBO stable** (bounded input ⇒ bounded output) if and only if $\sum_n \|h[n]\| < \infty$ (continuous: $\int \|h\| < \infty$);
-   **causal** (the output at time $t$ depends only on the past) if and only if $h[n] = 0$ for $n < 0$.

::: proof
Stability. (⇐) If $\|x\|_\infty \leq M$ then $\|y[n]\| \leq \sum_k \|x[k]\|\,\|h[n-k]\| \leq M \sum_k \|h[k]\|$: the convolution series converges absolutely. (⇒) Suppose $\sum \|h[n]\| = \infty$ and take the bounded input $x[k] = \mathrm{sign}(h[-k])$ ($\|x\| \leq 1$). Then $y[0] = \sum_k x[k]\,h[-k] = \sum_k \|h[k]\| = \infty$: the output explodes. Causality. (⇒) If $h[n_0] \neq 0$ for some $n_0 < 0$, the response to $\delta_0$ (a causal input, zero for $t < 0$) would be nonzero at $n_0 < 0$, before the impulse: contradiction. (⇐) If $h[n] = 0$ for $n < 0$, the sum $y[n] = \sum_{k \leq n} x[k]\,h[n-k]$ involves only $x[0], \dots, x[n]$.[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Proposition 1.4 — Frequency response: the exponentials are eigenvectors (proved)]{.tag} For a stable LTI system, the input $x(t) = e^{i2\pi\nu t}$ (a pure frequency) produces $y(t) = H(\nu)\,e^{i2\pi\nu t}$ with $$H(\nu) = \hat h(\nu) = \int h(\tau)\, e^{-i2\pi\nu\tau}\,d\tau.$$ $H$ is the **frequency response**: the system merely multiplies each frequency by a complex number (gain $\|H(\nu)\|$, phase $\arg H(\nu)$).

::: proof
$y(t) = \int h(\tau)\,x(t-\tau)\,d\tau = \int h(\tau)\,e^{i2\pi\nu(t-\tau)}\,d\tau = e^{i2\pi\nu t} \int h(\tau)\,e^{-i2\pi\nu\tau}\,d\tau$. The exponential comes out *unchanged* up to a complex factor: it is an eigenvector, with eigenvalue $H(\nu)$. This computational triviality is the heart of the whole course: filtering = multiplying the spectrum.[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 1.5 — Elementary convolutions]{.tag} Moving average ($h = \frac1M \mathbf{1}_{[0,M]}$): smooths, frequency response in $\mathrm{sinc}$; discrete differentiation ($h = \delta_{1} - \delta_0$): $H(\nu) = e^{-i2\pi\nu} - 1$, amplifies the high frequencies; integrator ($h = \mathbf{1}_{t \geq 0}$): unstable in the BIBO sense ($\int\|h\| = \infty$). A filter = a choice of $h$ (or of $H$); the whole of chapter 5 consists in *designing* $h$ from a desired $H$.
:::

## 2. The Fourier series {#ch2}

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.1 — Fourier series decomposition (coefficients by projection)]{.tag} Let $f$ be $T_0$-periodic, square integrable over one period. Then $$f = \sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} c_k\, e^{ik\omega_0 t} \quad \text{in } L^2, \qquad c_k = \frac{1}{T_0}\int_0^{T_0} f(t)\, e^{-ik\omega_0 t}\, dt,$$ the convergence taking place in $L^2$ norm (and pointwise toward $\frac{f(x^+)+f(x^-)}{2}$ at discontinuity points if $f$ is piecewise $C^1$: Dirichlet's theorem). The $c_k$ form the **spectrum**: $\|c_k\|$ magnitude, $\arg c_k$ phase.

::: proof
The $e_k = e^{ik\omega_0t}$ are orthogonal (prop. 0.1) and form a Hilbert basis (completeness, th. 0.3). The decomposition in an infinite orthonormal basis follows the logic of finite dimension: the partial sum $S_N f = \sum_{\|k\|\leq N} c_k e_k$ is the *orthogonal projection* of $f$ onto $\mathrm{Vect}\{e_k\}_{\|k\|\leq N}$, since $\langle f - S_Nf, e_j\rangle = 0$ for $\|j\| \leq N$. Since the basis is complete, $\|f - S_N f\|_{L^2} \to 0$. Explicitly: for every trigonometric polynomial $p = \sum_{\|k\|\leq N} d_k e_k$, Pythagoras gives $\|f - p\|^2 = \|f - S_Nf\|^2 + \|S_Nf - p\|^2 \geq \|f - S_Nf\|^2$: the projection is the best approximation — and the $d_k$ that cancel the cross terms are exactly $d_k = \langle f, e_k\rangle / \|e_k\|^2 = c_k$.[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.2 — Parseval's identity (proved by density)]{.tag} $$\frac{1}{T_0}\int_0^{T_0} \|f(t)\|^2\,dt = \sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} \|c_k\|^2.$$

::: proof
Pythagoras on $f = S_N f + (f - S_N f)$ with $\langle S_Nf, f - S_Nf\rangle = 0$: $\|f\|^2 = \|S_Nf\|^2 + \|f - S_Nf\|^2$. Now $\|S_Nf\|^2 = \sum_{\|k\|\leq N}\|c_k\|^2\|e_k\|^2 = T_0 \sum_{\|k\|\leq N}\|c_k\|^2$, and $\|f - S_Nf\|^2 \to 0$ by theorem 2.1 (whose proof rests on Fejér density, th. 0.3). Dividing by $T_0$ and passing to the limit, the "time" energy equals the "frequency" energy.[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Lemma 2.3 — Regularity and decay of the coefficients (by integrations by parts)]{.tag} If $f$ is $T_0$-periodic, piecewise $C^p$, with $f^{(p)}$ integrable, then $$c_k = \frac{1}{(ik\omega_0)^p}\, c_k\big(f^{(p)}\big), \qquad k \neq 0.$$ In particular: a jump discontinuity $[f]$ ⇒ $c_k \sim \frac{[f]}{T_0\,ik\omega_0} = \frac{[f]}{2i\pi k}$ (decay in $1/k$); $f$ piecewise $C^1$ ⇒ $c_k = O(1/k^2)$; $f$ $C^p$ ⇒ $c_k = o(1/k^p)$.

::: proof
Integration by parts over one period ($f$ piecewise $C^1$, the boundary terms cancel by periodicity): $c_k(f) = \frac{1}{T_0}\big[ f e^{-ik\omega_0t}\big]_0^{T_0} + \frac{ik\omega_0}{T_0}\int f(t)\,e^{-ik\omega_0t}dt = \frac{1}{ik\omega_0}c_k(f')$. One iterates $p$ times. The last term is a Fourier coefficient of an $L^2$ function (or of a jump if $f$ is discontinuous); Parseval (th. 2.2) applied to $f^{(p)}$ bounds $\sum \|c_k(f^{(p)})\|^2$, hence $c_k = o(k^{-p})$ since the series $\sum 1/k^{2p}$ must converge… and a residual jump imposes the exact $1/k$.[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 2.4 — The square wave: explicit coefficients and the Gibbs phenomenon]{.tag} For the odd square wave $f = \mathrm{sign}(\sin)$ (value ±1, jump of height 2): the direct computation (exercise 1, with solution) gives $$c_k = 0 \ (k \text{ even}), \qquad c_k = \frac{-2i}{\pi k} \ (k \text{ odd}) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(t) = \frac{4}{\pi}\sum_{m \geq 0} \frac{\sin\big((2m+1)\omega_0 t\big)}{2m+1}.$$ Decay in $1/k$, consistent with lemma 2.3 (discontinuity). The Gibbs phenomenon: near the jump, the partial sum $S_N f$ *overshoots* the target by about $$\Big(\frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi} \frac{\sin u}{u}\,du\Big) - \frac12 \approx 8.95\,\%$$ of the height of the jump, *whatever $N$*: the oscillation concentrates (width in $O(1/N)$) but its amplitude does not tend to 0. Origin: the Dirichlet kernel changes sign (ch. 0); by averaging (Fejér) or by windowing (ch. 5), the overshoot disappears — at the price of a widened transition.
:::

::: note
[Why these three results structure the whole course]{.tag} Parseval: the energy can be read in the spectrum (noise, filtering, SNR). Lemma 2.3: a smooth signal has a fast-decaying spectrum — the foundation of *compression* (one throws away the high frequencies) and of *sampling* (a fast-decaying spectrum is quickly negligible: ch. 4). Gibbs: any abrupt cutoff in frequency costs oscillations in time — hence the soft windows of ch. 5.
:::

## 3. The Fourier transform {#ch3}

::: def
[Definition 3.1 — The Fourier transform]{.tag} For $x \in L^1(\mathbb{R})$ (then $L^2$ by density): $$\hat x(\nu) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} x(t)\, e^{-i 2\pi \nu t}\, dt, \qquad x(t) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} \hat x(\nu)\, e^{i 2\pi \nu t}\, d\nu.$$ $\nu$ in Hz (or $\omega$ in rad/s with a factor $2\pi$); the "continuous" transform generalizes the Fourier coefficients to non- periodic signals: a signal of infinite duration has a continuous spectrum.
:::

:::: thm
[Proposition 3.2 — Fundamental properties (proved)]{.tag}

  Time                                  Frequency                              Proof (sketch)
  ------------------------------------- -------------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------
  delay $x(t - \tau)$                  $e^{-i2\pi\nu\tau}\hat x(\nu)$   change of variable $u = t-\tau$
  dilation $x(at)$                      $\frac1{\|a\|}\hat x(\nu/a)$        change of variable + axis reversal if $a < 0$
  modulation $x(t)e^{i2\pi\nu_0t}$   $\hat x(\nu - \nu_0)$               the exponentials compose
  derivative $x'$                       $i2\pi\nu\,\hat x$                 integration by parts, vanishing boundary terms
  convolution $x \* h$                  **product** $\hat x\,\hat h$        Fubini (see proof)
  product $x\,y$                       convolution $\hat x \* \hat y$       duality of the previous one
  Gaussian $e^{-\pi t^2}$            $e^{-\pi\nu^2}$                    see proposition 3.3

::: proof
*Convolution (via Fubini).* $\widehat{x\*h}(\nu) = \iint x(\tau)h(t-\tau)e^{-i2\pi\nu t}dt\,d\tau$. The modulus of the integrand is $\|x\|\,\|h\| \in L^1(\mathbb{R}^2)$ (a product of integrable functions), so Fubini allows the exchange; set $u = t - \tau$: $\int x(\tau)e^{-i2\pi\nu\tau}d\tau \cdot \int h(u)e^{-i2\pi\nu u}du = \hat x\,\hat h$. *Differentiation.* $\widehat{x'}(\nu) = [x e^{-i2\pi\nu t}] + i2\pi\nu\int x e^{-i2\pi\nu t}$ by parts; the boundary terms vanish for $x$ the derivative of an $L^1$ function. *Duality.* $\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{F}x)(t) = \int \hat x(\nu) e^{-i2\pi\nu t}d\nu = x(-t)$ (inversion formula evaluated at $-t$): Fourier² reverses time — hence product ↔ convolution by the previous property applied twice. *Dilation.* $u = at$: $\hat{}(at) = \int x(u)e^{-i2\pi\nu u/a}du/\|a\|$.[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Proposition 3.3 — The Gaussian is its own transform (computed)]{.tag} $$\mathcal{F}\big(e^{-\pi t^2}\big)(\nu) = e^{-\pi \nu^2}.$$

::: proof
Set $g(t) = e^{-\pi t^2}$ and consider $\hat g$. We exploit the differential equation $g' = -2\pi t\,g$. Integrating by parts, $\int t\,g(t)\,e^{-i2\pi\nu t}dt = -\frac{1}{2\pi}\int g'(t)\,e^{-i2\pi\nu t}dt = -\frac{1}{2\pi}\,i2\pi\nu\,\hat g = -i\nu\,\hat g$. Hence $\hat g'(\nu) = -i2\pi \int t g e^{-i2\pi\nu t} = -i2\pi(-i\nu)\hat g = -2\pi\nu\,\hat g$ — *the same differential equation*. Solution: $\hat g(\nu) = \hat g(0)\,e^{-\pi\nu^2}$, and $\hat g(0) = \int g = 1$ (Gaussian integral).[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[The key duo: convolution ↔ multiplication]{.tag} Filtering = convolving in time = *multiplying* in frequency: $y = x\*h \iff \hat y = \hat x\,H$, where $H(\nu) = \hat h(\nu)$ is the **frequency response** (prop. 1.4). Low-pass: $H \approx 1$ for $\|\nu\| < \nu_c$, $\approx 0$ beyond. This is also why the FFT speeds up the convolutions of CNNs: complexity $\mathcal{O}(n \log n)$ instead of $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ (see the Deep Learning module). With proposition 3.3, a "narrow" Gaussian in time is "wide" in frequency — a foretaste of the next theorem.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.4 — Heisenberg-Gabor uncertainty (proved)]{.tag} For $x$ of energy 1, with standard deviations $\sigma_t$ (time, around $t_0$) and $\sigma_\nu$ (frequency): $$\sigma_t \, \sigma_\nu \ \geq\ \frac{1}{4\pi},$$ with **equality if and only if** $x$ is a Gaussian (modulated and translated).

::: proof
Time translations and frequency modulations do not change the product $\sigma_t\sigma_\nu$ (delay = pure phase; modulation = a translation of the spectrum): one assumes $t_0 = \nu_0 = 0$, $\|x\|_2 = 1$. Let us derive the key identity by parts (vanishing boundary terms): $\int t\,\frac{d}{dt}\|x\|^2 dt = -\int \|x\|^2 = -1$, and $\frac{d}{dt}\|x\|^2 = 2\mathrm{Re}(x\,\overline{x'})$, hence $2\,\mathrm{Re}\langle t\,x, x'\rangle = 1$, i.e. $\|\langle tx, x'\rangle\| \geq 1/2$. Cauchy-Schwarz: $\tfrac12 \leq \|t x\|_2\,\|x'\|_2 = \sigma_t\,\|x'\|_2$. Finally $\|x'\|_2^2 = \|\widehat{x'}\|_2^2 = \|i2\pi\nu\,\hat x\|_2^2 = (2\pi\sigma_\nu)^2$ (Parseval + differentiation). Hence $\sigma_t\sigma_\nu \geq 1/(4\pi)$. Equality: Cauchy-Schwarz must be saturated, $x' = \lambda t x$: the solutions are the Gaussians $e^{-\pi t^2/\sigma^2}$ (up to a linear phase and a translation).[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 3.5 — Useful distributions: Dirac and comb]{.tag} Without formalism: the Dirac mass $\delta$ is "the function" of mass 1 concentrated at 0, defined by $\int f\,\delta = f(0)$ (a distribution, i.e. a continuous linear form on test functions). We admit: $\hat\delta = 1$, $\hat 1 = \delta$ (duality), and the **Dirac comb** $\,\Sha_{T_e}(t) = \sum_n \delta(t - nT_e)$, whose transform is a comb: $$\widehat{\Sha_{T_e}}(\nu) = \frac{1}{T_e}\,\Sha_{1/T_e}(\nu).$$ These objects make rigorous: the spectrum of a sinusoid (two $\delta$ lines), sampling (a product with a comb, ch. 4), white noise (ch. 7).
:::

## 4. Sampling: the Shannon theorem {#ch4}

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.1 — Shannon-Nyquist (proved)]{.tag} Let $x$ be band-limited: $\hat x(\nu) = 0$ for $\|\nu\| \geq B$, and $f_s = 1/T_e > 2B$. Then the samples $x_n = x(nT_e)$ suffice to reconstruct *exactly* $x$: $$x(t) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} x_n\, \mathrm{sinc}\Big(\frac{t}{T_e} - n\Big), \qquad \mathrm{sinc}(u) = \frac{\sin(\pi u)}{\pi u}.$$

::: proof
**Step 1 (sampling = periodizing the spectrum).** Ideal sampling is written $x_s(t) = x(t)\cdot\Sha_{T_e}(t) = \sum_n x_n\,\delta(t - nT_e)$. Product in time ⇒ convolution in frequency (prop. 3.2): $$\hat x_s(\nu) = \hat x \* \widehat{\Sha_{T_e}}(\nu) = \frac{1}{T_e}\sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} \hat x\Big(\nu - \frac{k}{T_e}\Big).$$ The spectrum of $x_s$ is the *periodization* of the spectrum of $x$, of period $f_s$. **Step 2 (no overlap).** If $f_s > 2B$, the copies (centered at $0, \pm f_s, \pm 2f_s, \dots$, each of half-width $B$) are disjoint: in the central band $\|\nu\| < f_s/2$ we read $\hat x = T_e\,\hat x_s$. **Step 3 (ideal low-pass filtering).** Let us multiply by $R(\nu) = T_e\,\mathbf{1}_{\|\nu\| < f_s/2}$: $\hat x = R\,\hat x_s$, that is, $x = r \* x_s$ where $r = \check R$ is the inverse transform of the rectangle — computed by direct integration: $r(t) = T_e\int_{-f_s/2}^{f_s/2} e^{i2\pi\nu t}d\nu = \frac{\sin(\pi f_s t)}{\pi f_s t}\cdot f_s T_e = \mathrm{sinc}(f_s t)$. **Step 4 (interpolation formula).** Convolving sinc with the comb of samples gives, since $\mathrm{sinc}\big(f_s(t - nT_e)\big) = \mathrm{sinc}(f_st - n)$ and since the sinc equals 1 at 0 and 0 at the other integers (the samples do not "talk" to each other): $$x(t) = \sum_n x_n\, \mathrm{sinc}(f_s t - n).\qquad\qquad \square$$ If $f_s \leq 2B$, the copies overlap: the information is lost without return (two different signals have the same samples).[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: prop
[Proposition 4.2 — Aliasing, in formulas]{.tag} After sampling at $f_s$, every frequency $\nu$ is seen at the *apparent* frequency $$\nu_{\text{app}} = \min_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}\ \big\|\nu - k f_s\big\| \ \in\ \Big[0, \frac{f_s}{2}\Big],$$ the image of $\nu$ in the fundamental band $[-f_s/2, f_s/2]$ modulo $f_s$. Example: $f_s = 80$ Hz, $\nu = 60$ Hz ⇒ $\nu_{\text{app}} = \|60 - 80\| = 20$ Hz (the line "moves backward"); a rising chirp passes $f_s/2$, then *goes back down* — the ghost trace of the spectrogram of exercise 6. Wheels that seem to turn backward in the movies, moiré of images: the same phenomenon.
:::

::: note
[Bandpass sampling]{.tag} For a signal modulating only a *narrow band* $[f_c - B, f_c + B]$ (radio, sensors), the useful condition bears on the width $2B$ and not on the highest frequency: it suffices to choose $f_s$ such that the copies of the band do not overlap. Example: band $[19, 21]$ MHz ($f_c = 20$, $B = 1$), $f_s = 4$ MHz: every frequency $f$ folds back to $\|f - 20\|$ MHz, without collision — the spectrum is transposed to baseband, possibly flipped (spectral reversal depending on the parity of the multiple of $f_s$). This is the basis of software receivers (SDR).
:::

::: ex
[Example 4.3 — Acquisition chain and practical reconstruction]{.tag} Chain: analog signal → analog *anti-aliasing* filter (cuts at $f_s/2$, indispensable *before* sampling) → sampling $f_s$ → quantization ($b$ bits: quantization noise at $\approx 6b$ dB of dynamic range) → digital. Audio CD: $B = 20$ kHz ⇒ $f_s = 44.1$ kHz, 16 bits. The Shannon sinc is perfectly localized in frequency but infinitely long in time: one *truncates and windows* it (sinc × Hann over $M$ points) — hence a slight aliasing and a soft transition, quantifiable with the tools of ch. 5; linear interpolation (triangle) is its cheap version.
:::

```python
import numpy as np
fs = 200                       # sampling frequency
t  = np.arange(0, 1, 1/fs)
f0 = 60                        # signal 60 Hz
x  = np.sin(2*np.pi*f0*t)

X = np.fft.rfft(x)             # spectrum (positive frequencies)
freqs = np.fft.rfftfreq(len(x), 1/fs)
peak = freqs[np.argmax(np.abs(X))]
print("frequence dominante :", peak, "Hz")

# Aliasing: sampling a 60 Hz signal at 80 Hz "sees" it at 20 Hz
fs2 = 80; t2 = np.arange(0, 1, 1/fs2)
x2 = np.sin(2*np.pi*f0*t2)
print("vu a :", np.fft.rfftfreq(len(x2),1/fs2)[np.argmax(np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x2)))], "Hz")

# Shannon reconstruction on a fine grid (sinc truncated to the 21 neighbors)
tr = np.arange(0, 1, 1/2000); xr = np.zeros_like(tr)
for n in range(len(x)):
    xr += x[n]*np.sinc(fs*tr - n)
print("erreur max apres reconstruction :", np.abs(np.sin(2*np.pi*f0*tr) - xr).max())
```

## 5. DFT, FFT and digital filtering {#ch5}

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — The DFT]{.tag} For $x_0, \dots, x_{N-1}$: $$X_k = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x_n\, e^{-i 2\pi k n / N}, \qquad k = 0, \dots, N-1.$$ The DFT samples the transform of the implicitly *periodized* signal ($k \leftrightarrow \nu_k = k f_s/N$). Two links to know:

-   **DFT ↔ Fourier series**: if $x$ is $T_0$-periodic sampled with $N$ points *per period* and $f_s > 2B$: $X_k = N\,c_k$ (for $k < N/2$, and $X_{N-k} = N c_{-k}$);
-   **DFT ↔ Fourier transform**: for a segment of duration $T = NT_e$ of an aperiodic signal: $\hat x(\nu_k) \approx T_e\,X_k$ (the so-called "rectangular" approximation, with the spectral leakage of prop. 5.4).
:::

:::: thm
[Proposition 5.2 — Circular convolution (proved)]{.tag} Let $x \circledast h$ be the *circular* convolution (indices modulo $N$): $y_n = \sum_{m=0}^{N-1} x_m\,h_{(n-m) \bmod N}$. Then $\mathrm{DFT}(x \circledast h)_k = X_k\,H_k$.

::: proof
$Y_k = \sum_n \sum_m x_m h_{(n-m) \bmod N}\,\omega^{kn}$ with $\omega = e^{-2\pi i/N}$. For $m$ fixed, $n \mapsto p = (n-m) \bmod N$ is a bijection of $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ and $\omega^{kn} = \omega^{k(m+p)}$ (since $\omega^{kN} = 1$). Hence $Y_k = \sum_m x_m\omega^{km}\sum_p h_p\omega^{kp} = X_k H_k$. The *linear* convolution is obtained by **zero-padding** both signals to $N' \geq n + m - 1$ points: the "circular" wrap-around then no longer has any effect (the overflowing indices fall on zeros).[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.3 — Radix-2 FFT (proved: the butterfly recurrence)]{.tag} If $N = 2^q$, the DFT is computed in $T(N) = \mathcal{O}(N \log N)$ operations.

::: proof
Separate the even and odd sums: $$X_k = \underbrace{\sum_{m=0}^{N/2-1} x_{2m}\,\omega^{2mk}}_{E_k} +\ \omega^{k}\,\underbrace{\sum_{m=0}^{N/2-1} x_{2m+1}\,\omega^{2mk}}_{O_k}.$$ Now $\omega^2 = e^{-4\pi i/N}$ is an $N/2$-th root of unity: $E$ and $O$ are two DFTs of size $N/2$, *periodic* with period $N/2$; and $\omega^{k + N/2} = -\omega^k$. Hence the **butterfly**: $$X_k = E_k + \omega^k O_k, \qquad X_{k+N/2} = E_k - \omega^k O_k, \qquad k = 0,\dots,\tfrac{N}{2}-1,$$ which produces the $N$ outputs from the $N$ inputs in $O(N)$ multiply-adds once $E, O$ are known. Recurrence $T(N) = 2T(N/2) + cN = cN\log_2 N$. For $N = 2^{20}$ (one second of audio): $\approx 2\times10^7$ units versus $10^{12}$ for the definition — a factor of 50,000.[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: prop
[Proposition 5.4 — Windows: quantified lobes]{.tag} Analyzing a segment of signal = multiplying it by a window $w$ ⇒ convolving the spectrum with $\hat w$ (prop. 3.2): a pure line becomes the profile $\hat w$. Characteristics (window of length $M$, bin $= f_s/M$, classical values of Harris 1978):

  Window        Main lobe   1st side lobe   Decay
  ------------- ----------- --------------- ---------------
  rectangular   ±1 bin      −13 dB          −6 dB/octave
  Hann          ±2 bins     −31 dB          −18 dB/octave
  Hamming       ±2 bins     −41 dB          −6 dB/octave
  Blackman      ±3 bins     −58 dB          −18 dB/octave

Universal trade-off: a narrow window (low side lobes) ⇒ a wide main lobe (resolution lost). The rectangular one "leaks" at −13 dB: a strong line masks a weak neighboring line at −60 dB; Hann is the default choice.
:::

::: def
[Digital filters: FIR and IIR]{.tag} **FIR** (finite impulse response): $y_n = \sum_{k=0}^{M} b_k x_{n-k}$ — always stable (Σ\|b\| finite: th. 1.3), linear phase if the $b_k$ are symmetric, designed by windowing; **IIR** (infinite): $y_n = \sum b_k x_{n-k} - \sum_{j\geq1} a_j y_{n-j}$, transfer function $H(z) = B(z)/A(z)$ — more selective at equal coefficient counts, but stability must be checked.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.5 — Stability of an IIR: the poles (proved)]{.tag} For a rational IIR, BIBO stable ⇔ all the poles of $H(z)$ lie in the open disk $\|z\| < 1$.

::: proof
The impulse response of a system with (simple) poles $p_1, \dots, p_r$ is a combination of $\mathcal{O}(n^s)\,p_j^n$: each mode contributes $\sum_n \|p_j\|^n$, a geometric series convergent ⇔ $\|p_j\| < 1$. A pole on the unit disk ⇒ a marginal or divergent mode; outside ⇒ a divergent exponential (the accumulator $h = \mathbf{1}$, pole at 1, illustrates this).[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 5.6 — Designing a low-pass FIR by windowing, step by step]{.tag} Objective: $H_d(\nu) = \mathbf{1}_{\|\nu\| \leq \nu_c}$ (ν normalized by $f_s$).

1.  **Ideal response in time**: $h_d[n] = 2\nu_c\,\mathrm{sinc}(2\nu_c n)$ (inverse FT of the rectangle, cf. proof of th. 4.1) — infinite and non-causal.
2.  **Delay** of $M/2$ for causality (and symmetry ⇒ linear phase).
3.  **Windowing**: $h[n] = h_d[n - M/2]\,w[n - M/2]$, $n = 0,\dots,M$.
4.  **Analysis**: $H = H_d \* \hat w$; the transition band equals the width of the main lobe of $\hat w$ — rule of thumb $M \cdot \Delta\nu \approx 4$ (Hann), $\approx 6$ (Blackman); the in-band ripple equals the level of the side lobes (prop. 5.4).

The **effective frequency response** is the DTFT of $h$, $H(\nu) = \sum_n h[n]e^{-2\pi i\nu n}$, evaluated by zero-padding the FFT (trick: a DFT with $N_{\text{fft}} \gg M$ points interpolates the DTFT). A finer alternative: **frequency-domain least squares** — minimize $\sum_{\omega \in \Omega} \|H_b(\omega) - D(\omega)\|^2$ over a frequency grid, a quadratic problem in $b$, hence a linear system (Parks-McClellan equiripple method: the same spirit in infinite norm). For IIRs, one projects an analog prototype via the **bilinear transform** $s \mapsto \frac{2}{T_e}\frac{1 - z^{-1}}{1 + z^{-1}}$ (Butterworth, Chebyshev…) while keeping the poles inside the disk — the "smooth" filter of example 5.7.
:::

::: ex
[Example 5.7 — Low-pass denoising]{.tag}

```python
sig = x + 0.5*rng.standard_normal(len(x))
SIG = np.fft.rfft(sig)
SIG[np.abs(freqs) > 80] = 0            # abrupt cutoff at 80 Hz (zero-phase)
clean = np.fft.irfft(SIG, n=len(sig))
# Abrupt cutoff in frequency = Gibbs in time (th. 2.4): prefer a soft
# profile (4th-order Butterworth via scipy.signal.butter + filtfilt, or a Hann mask)
```
:::

## 6. Time-frequency analysis and wavelets {#ch6}

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — STFT and spectrogram]{.tag} $$\mathrm{STFT}_x(t, \nu) = \int x(\tau)\, w(\tau - t)\, e^{-i2\pi\nu\tau}\, d\tau,$$ with $w$ a short window (Hann). The **spectrogram** $\|\mathrm{STFT}_x\|^2$ describes the energy across time *and* frequency: it is the image of sound that a convolutional network "sees" (ch. 8).
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 6.2 — Exact resolution of the STFT]{.tag} At each instant, the STFT is the FT of the windowed segment $x\cdot w(\cdot - t)$: its frequency resolution is the width of the main lobe of $\hat w$ (prop. 5.4); its time resolution is the duration $T$ of the window. For Hann: main lobe $\pm 2/T$ in frequency, hence $$\Delta t = T, \qquad \Delta\nu \approx \frac{2}{T} \ \ (\text{Hann}), \qquad \Delta t\,\Delta\nu \approx 2,$$ to be compared with the floor $1/(4\pi) \approx 0.08$ (standard deviations) of th. 3.4: the STFT works at a resolution *fixed in advance*, far from the floor, but with time-frequency cells all identical. Long window ⇒ good frequency resolution, poor time resolution — and conversely: the trade-off is *irreversible* for a given window.
:::

::: note
[Gabor frames: sampling the STFT]{.tag} A continuously stored STFT is redundant; one samples it on a grid $(t,\nu) = (m\,a,\ n\,b)$. Results (admitted): if $ab < 1$ (a fine enough grid), the family of translated-modulated windows $w_{m,n}$ forms a **Gabor frame**: stable reconstruction by a dual window; at the critical density $ab = 1$, no well-localized orthonormal basis exists (the Balian-Low theorem): one must accept redundancy (or change the geometry: wavelets below). This is exactly the structure of spectrograms: frames every 10 ms, $N$ frequencies — a frame, not a basis.
:::

::: def
[Definition 6.3 — Wavelets: analysis at variable scale]{.tag} Mother wavelet $\psi$ (zero mean, localized); $\psi_{a,b}(t) = \frac1{\sqrt a}\psi\big(\frac{t-b}{a}\big)$; the CWT samples $(a,b)$, often in octaves $a = 2^{-j}$ (**scalogram**, $Q = \Delta\nu/\nu$ constant): good time localization at high frequency, frequency localization at low frequency — suited to sounds (closely spaced harmonics at the bottom of the spectrum, brief transients at the top), where the STFT is uniform.
:::

::: ex
[Example 6.4 — Haar, a complete example down to reconstruction]{.tag} The Haar wavelet: $\varphi = \mathbf{1}_{[0,1)}$ (scale), $\psi = \mathbf{1}_{[0,1/2)} - \mathbf{1}_{[1/2,1)}$ (detail). Signal $x = (9, 7, 3, 5)$:

-   level 1: averages $a_1 = (8, 4)$, details $d_1 = (1, -1)$;
-   level 2: $a_2 = (6)$, $d_2 = (2)$;
-   coding: $x \leftrightarrow (a_2, d_2, d_1) = (6, 2, 1, -1)$; reconstruction: $9 = 6+2+1$, $7 = 6+2-1$, $3 = 6-2+1$, $5 = 6-2-1$.

The **multiresolution** equations: $\varphi(t) = \sqrt2\sum_k h_k\varphi(2t-k)$, $\psi(t) = \sqrt2\sum_k g_k\varphi(2t-k)$; for Haar, $h = (\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}, \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2})$, $g = (\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}, -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2})$ — $h$ = averaging filter (low-pass), $g$ = differentiator (high-pass). The **Daubechies $D_N$** compactify this scheme with $2N$ coefficients and $N$ *vanishing moments*: on a piecewise regular signal, the detail coefficients decay like $2^{-Nj}$ — this is what makes the coding sparse (a polynomial of degree < N has *exactly* zero details: Haar = $D_1$ annihilates constants).
:::

::: note
[DWT = a filter bank, and the JPEG 2000 link]{.tag} The DWT is implemented without any integral: a cascade of low-pass ($h$) / high-pass ($g$) filterings followed by decimation by a factor 2, iterated on the low branch; the "quadrature mirror" conditions on $(h,g)$ cancel the aliasing introduced by the decimations. JPEG 2000 codes the subbands of a biorthogonal DWT (5/3 lossless, 9/7 lossy): an image = a 2D signal, and compression exploits lemma 2.3 (regularity ⇒ small coefficients). Same bank, from denoising to compression: the theory does not change.
:::

## 7. Random signals and spectral estimation {#ch7}

::: def
[Definition 7.1 — Process, wide-sense stationarity (WSS)]{.tag} A **random signal** is a family $X(t, \omega)$ of random variables. It is *wide-sense stationary* if its mean is constant $m = \mathbb{E}[X(t)]$ and if its **autocorrelation** $$R_X(t, t+\tau) = \mathbb{E}\big[(X(t)-m)\,\overline{(X(t+\tau)-m)}\big]$$ depends only on the lag $\tau$ (written $R_X(\tau)$). This is the right framework for noise, speech, sensors: each realization is a signal of this course, but the interesting quantities are expectations.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 7.2 — Properties of the autocorrelation]{.tag} $R_X(0) = \mathbb{E}\|X - m\|^2$ is the **average power**; $\|R_X(\tau)\| \leq R_X(0)$ (Cauchy-Schwarz: $\|\mathbb{E}[X_0\overline{X_\tau}]\| \leq \sqrt{R(0)R(0)}$); $R_X$ is hermitian ($R_X(-\tau) = \overline{R_X(\tau)}$) and positive definite. "Noise" is decorrelated at a distance: $R(\tau) \to 0$.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 7.3 — Wiener-Khinchin (statement) and the spectral density]{.tag} For a WSS process, there exists a positive measure $S_X$, the **power spectral density**, such that $$R_X(\tau) = \int e^{i2\pi\nu\tau}\, dS_X(\nu), \qquad\text{and if } R_X \in L^1:\quad S_X(\nu) = \widehat{R_X}(\nu).$$ The power is distributed across the spectrum: $\mathbb{E}\|X-m\|^2 = R_X(0) = \int dS_X$: Parseval (th. 2.2) becomes a *definition*. (The proof — Bochner's theorem — goes beyond the scope of the course; the intuition: a WSS process is an incoherent superposition of sinusoids, each carrying its share of the power.)

-   **White noise**: decorrelated to all orders, $R = \sigma^2\delta$ ⇒ $S = \sigma^2$ constant — "all frequencies on equal footing". A *band-limited* white noise (physically realizable): $S = \sigma^2\mathbf{1}_{\|\nu\| \leq B}$ ⇒ $R(\tau) = 2B\sigma^2\,\mathrm{sinc}(2B\tau)$: decorrelation at the scale $1/B$ (direct computation of the FT of the rectangle, cf. th. 4.1).
-   **Filtered noise**: $Y = h \* X$ ⇒ $S_Y = \|H\|^2\,S_X$ (colored noise): the filter shapes the spectrum *squared*.
-   **AR(1)** (auto-regressive model $X_n = \rho X_{n-1} + W_n$, $\|\rho\| < 1$): $R[\tau] = \frac{\sigma_W^2}{1-\rho^2}\,\rho^{\|\tau\|}$ and $S(\nu) = \frac{\sigma_W^2}{\|1 - \rho e^{-i2\pi\nu}\|^2}$ — the simplest model of colored noise, ubiquitous in finance and sensors.
:::

::: def
[Definition 7.4 — The periodogram]{.tag} "Natural" estimator of $S_X$ from $N$ samples: $$\hat S_N(\nu) = \frac{1}{N}\Big\|\sum_{n<N} X_n\, e^{-i2\pi\nu n}\Big\|^2 \qquad (\text{on the DFT grid: } \|X_k\|^2/N).$$
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 7.5 — Bias and variance of the periodogram]{.tag}

-   **Bias (leakage)**: $\mathbb{E}[\hat S_N] = S \* W_N$ where $W_N$ is the Dirichlet kernel (prop. 0.2): the expectation "smears" over ±1 bin — a strong line masks a weak line (hence the windows, prop. 5.4). The bias tends to 0 as $N \to \infty$ ($W_N \to \delta$).
-   **Variance**: for a Gaussian process, $\mathrm{Var}[\hat S_N(\nu)] \approx S_X(\nu)^2$ for every $N$ — the relative error is 100% *and does not decrease*: the periodogram alone is a poor estimator, whatever the observation duration.

::: proof
Sketch. Bias: $\hat S_N = \widehat{z_N}\,\overline{\widehat{z_N}}$ with $z_N = X\cdot w_N$ (truncation = rectangular window); the product in time becomes a convolution of the spectrum with $\hat w_N = W_N$ (prop. 3.2), then one takes the expectation. Variance: on the DFT grid, the $\hat S_N(\nu_k)$ are asymptotically decorrelated and, for a Gaussian, $\hat S_N(\nu)$ approximately follows $S(\nu)\cdot \chi^2_2/2$ (squared modulus of two independent Gaussians); now $\mathrm{Var}[\chi^2_2/2] = 1$, hence a variance of order $S^2$, independent of $N$.[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Bartlett and Welch methods — reducing the variance by averaging]{.tag}

-   **Bartlett**: split the $N$ points into $L$ disjoint segments of $M = N/L$ points and average the periodograms: $\mathrm{Var} \approx S^2/L$… at the price of an increased bias (windows $M$ times shorter ⇒ leakage multiplied) — the central bias/variance trade-off of spectral estimation.
-   **Welch**: *overlapping* segments (50%) and Hann windows: the same variance gain (Hann segments overlap "for free"), leakage controlled at −31 dB; this is the default method of instrumentation.

```python
from scipy.signal import welch
n  = 20000; fs = 500.0
t  = np.arange(n)/fs
x  = np.sin(2*np.pi*50*t) + 0.02*np.sin(2*np.pi*80*t) + 0.5*rng.standard_normal(n)

f, S = welch(x, fs=fs, nperseg=1024, window='hann', noverlap=512)
# L = 2*20000/1024 - 1 segments: the line at 80 Hz (-34 dB below the line at 50 Hz)
# emerges from the noise, whereas the raw periodogram drowns it (th. 7.5)
```
:::

::: note
[Complement to the official syllabus: Wiener filtering]{.tag} The detailed syllabus of the course unit explicitly mentions "filtering and prediction of stationary random signals" and "Wiener filtering": here is the object. We observe $Y = X + W$ (signal $X$ WSS, noise $W$ WSS, with spectra $S_X, S_W$, assumed uncorrelated) and we seek the LTI filter $h$ that minimizes the mean squared error $\mathbb{E}\|X - h \* Y\|^2$. The (non-causal) solution is the **Wiener filter**: $$H(\nu) = \frac{S_X(\nu)}{S_X(\nu) + S_W(\nu)}.$$ Reading: at frequencies where the signal dominates ($S_X \gg S_W$) the filter transmits ($H \approx 1$); where the noise dominates, it cancels out — the spectrum decides, optimally in the $L^2$ sense. This is exactly the "filtered noise" of Theorem 7.3 ($S_Y = \|H\|^2 S_X$) inverted: instead of *computing* the effect of a filter on a spectrum, we *design* the filter that best separates signal and noise, from their estimated spectral densities (Definition 7.4 and Theorem 7.5 — estimated in practice by Bartlett/Welch). The causal filter is built by spectral factorization (via the transfer function $H(z)$ of ch. 5); the linear prediction of an AR process (the $X_n = \rho X_{n-1} + W_n$ of Theorem 7.3) is its "zero noise" case: predicting is filtering toward the future. The Kalman filter is its recursive state-space variant, seen in the downstream modules of the program.
:::

## 8. The signal for modern ML {#ch8}

::: thm
[Mel spectrogram and MFCC: the standard pipeline]{.tag}

1.  **Frames**: 25 ms cuts every 10 ms, Hann window (a Gabor frame, ch. 6); STFT.
2.  **Mel scale** (perceptive, linear < 1 kHz then logarithmic): $$m = 2595\,\log_{10}\Big(1 + \frac{f}{700}\Big), \qquad f = 700\,\big(10^{m/2595} - 1\big).$$
3.  **Mel filter bank**: 20-80 triangular filters with edges uniformly spaced *in Mel* — band-pass filters of increasing width in Hz: $E_m = \sum_\nu W_m(\nu)\,\|\mathrm{STFT}(\nu)\|^2$ (a sparse weighting of the spectrogram).
4.  **Log** (amplitude perception); **DCT** along the Mel axis (a DCT = a "real FT"): the $c_j$ are the **MFCC**; one keeps 13-20 coefficients + derivatives $\Delta, \Delta\Delta$, and normalizes in mean/variance per speaker.

Historically *features* for lightweight models (GMM-HMM), the MFCC remain the compact entry point; deep networks rather consume the raw **Mel spectrogram**.
:::

::: note
[Networks on spectrograms]{.tag} The Mel spectrogram is *the image* that 2D CNNs and audio transformers consume: the first layers of audio CNNs learn oriented frequency detectors — Gabor filters (ch. 6), see the Deep Learning module. The emblematic data augmentation (masking of frequency bands and time frames) operates directly *in the time-frequency plane*: the spectrogram is treated as a texture to be repaired. Speech technology, transcription, audio-multimodal transformers: this whole pipeline is the signal preprocessing of modern ML.
:::

::: thm
[Distances between spectral distributions: FID and OT spectral loss]{.tag} Comparing two sets of signals = comparing two distributions of spectrograms (or of features). Standard: fit a Gaussian to the features of each set and measure the **Fréchet distance** $$d^2\big(\mathcal{N}(\mu_1,\Sigma_1), \mathcal{N}(\mu_2,\Sigma_2)\big) = \|\mu_1 - \mu_2\|^2 + \mathrm{tr}\Big(\Sigma_1 + \Sigma_2 - 2\big(\Sigma_1^{1/2}\Sigma_2\Sigma_1^{1/2}\big)^{1/2}\Big).$$ This is *nothing but* $W_2^2$ between Gaussians (the Bures metric): the FID of image generators and the "audio Fréchet distance" of audio generators are Wasserstein distances in disguise. The **OT spectral loss** of audio generative models generalizes the idea: comparing real/generated batches by Gaussian $W_2$ (closed form above, differentiable) or by Sinkhorn on the spectra: the *complete proof* of the Bures formula and the Sinkhorn algorithm are on the syllabus of the *Computational Optimal Transport* module (M1P2, ch. 2 and 3, same instructor) — this chapter is its preparation. In 1D (spectra or one-dimensional signals), everything reduces to the quantile coupling: $W_2^2 = \int_0^1\big(F_1^{-1}(u) - F_2^{-1}(u)\big)^2du$ (proved there).
:::

::: ex
[Example 8.1 — 1D domain adaptation on signals]{.tag} Two sensors measure the same phenomenon with different drifts (offset, gain, frequency response): the *distributions* of the frames differ, not the semantics. Alignment by 1D OT: transport the quantiles of sensor A onto those of sensor B (monotone transport, computable by sorting); the same principle at d-dimensional scale (feature clouds) is the *optimal transport domain adaptation* detailed in the OT module (ch. 4), whose instructor is a co-author. The signal provides the spectrum; OT provides the geometry.
:::

::: note
[Fourier in the architectures: convolutions and positions]{.tag}

-   **Convolution of CNNs** = the discrete convolution of ch. 1: the learned kernel is a filter whose frequency response (DTFT, ch. 5) explains its behavior — CNNs learn banks of Gabor filters; convolution via FFT in $\mathcal{O}(n\log n)$ when the kernels are large (th. 5.3).
-   **Convolution on graphs**: the GNN message passing $h \leftarrow \sigma(\tilde D^{-1/2}\tilde A \tilde D^{-1/2} h W)$ is a convolution in the spectral sense — the Kipf & Welling filter is a degree-1 polynomial of the Laplacian; expanded in the Graph ML module.
-   **Positional encodings**: the sine/cosine of transformers ($\mathrm{PE}(p, 2i) = \sin(p/10000^{2i/d})$…) = Fourier bases; positional encodings on graphs (LapEig) reuse the eigenvectors of the Laplacian — Fourier again, see the Graph ML module.
:::

::: note
[Complement to the official syllabus: source separation and the learning dictionary]{.tag} The "Signal representation and learning dictionary" block of the detailed syllabus of the course unit names **source separation** and the **learning dictionary**: here is the principle. The idea — officially that of the course — is to move from fixed bases (Fourier, wavelets, ch. 2 and 6) to a *learned dictionary*: a signal is represented as $x \approx D\alpha$ with $D = [d_1 \| \dots \| d_K]$ a dictionary of waveforms and $\alpha$ **sparse** (few active coefficients). Learning $D$ (for instance by non-negative matrix factorization — NMF — or K-SVD-type sparse least squares) on spectrograms of mixtures separates the sources: each component $d_k\alpha_k$ concentrates on one source (a speaker, an instrument), since a mixture is a *sum* of sources and sparsity forces the atoms to specialize. This is the first historical bridge between signal processing and unsupervised learning: a learned dictionary is a latent representation, $\alpha$ a code — the same grammar as the autoencoders of the Deep Learning module, with the added spectral interpretability of the atoms. The "deep learning" signal reconstruction announced by the sheet is the generalization of this scheme in which the decoder becomes a network trained on degraded/clean pairs (denoising, super-resolution).
:::

## 9. The teacher's research: from signals to optimal transport {#ch9}

::: note
[Who teaches this module, and why it is no accident]{.tag} Rémi Flamary (CMAP, École Polytechnique) is co-director of the LLGA master's program and co-creator of the [POT — Python Optimal Transport](https://pythonot.github.io) library (JMLR 2021): one of the most used tools in the field. His research connects precisely the two ends of this course: from signals and images (telecommunications, brain imaging) to distances between *distributions* of data — that is, from the spectrograms of this module to the OT losses of the M1P2 module.
:::

::: thm
[POT: a library designed for lab practice]{.tag} Architecture (introductory session):

-   **Exact solvers**: `ot.emd` (network simplex, exact LP); **regularized**: `ot.sinkhorn` and its log-stabilized version; **structured**: `ot.gromov` (GW, FGW); **barycenters**; **domain adaptation**: `ot.da.OTDA` — the transported classifier of the TPAMI 2016 paper, packaged.
-   **Native backpropagation**: the NumPy/PyTorch/JAX backends — an OT loss (*spectral loss* included) fits into any training loop; the gradient of the regularized cost is the dual potential (proved in the OT module, ch. 3).
-   **Impact**: \~80 solvers from the literature, a gallery of examples, used from medical to generative audio: the "de facto standard" of numerical OT.
:::

::: ex
[Bridging lab: optimal transport between two segments of a spectrogram]{.tag}

```python
import numpy as np, ot
import scipy.signal as sig

fs = 8000; t = np.arange(2*fs)/fs
x  = np.sin(2*np.pi*440*t) + 0.5*rng.random(2*fs)      # two "notes" with noise
f, T, S = sig.stft(x, fs=fs, nperseg=512, window='hann')

A = np.abs(S[:, T[0] < 0.5]).ravel()                   # spectra t < 0.5 s
B = np.abs(S[:, T[0] >= 0.5]).ravel()                  # spectra t >= 0.5 s
a, b = np.ones(len(A))/len(A), np.ones(len(B))/len(B)
Ca = A[:, None]*A[:, None] + 1e-9                      # cost: "close" spectra
G  = ot.sinkhorn(a, b, ot.dist(A[:,None], B[:,None]), reg=0.05)
# Matplotlib visualization described: ot.plot.plot1D_mat(A, B, G, "transport plan")
# -- the mass connects the spectra of the same contour; compare with simple correlation
```

One "transports" the distribution of the spectra of one half toward the other: this is exactly the basic building block of the spectral losses of generative audio ML (ch. 8), and the first lab of the M1P2 module.
:::

::: note
[A recent bridge: projections, sliced OT and reconstruction]{.tag} Part of the instructor's recent work deals with *sliced* transport (random 1D projections): Tanguy, Flamary & Delon, "Reconstructing discrete measures from projections" (C. R. Mathématique, 2024 — [arXiv:2304.12029](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.12029)) show how the projections of a discrete measure determine it, with consequences for the empirical sliced Wasserstein distance. The vocabulary is that of the course: projecting a cloud (a measure of spectrograms) onto directions means computing *marginal spectra*; 1D OT by quantiles (ch. 8) does the rest. Flamary's other works (FGW, domain adaptation, COOT) are detailed in the *Computational Optimal Transport* module (M1P2, ch. 7).
:::

## Exercises {#ex}

1.  **Square wave series (with solution).** Compute the $c_k$ of the odd square wave $f = \mathrm{sign}(\sin)$, check the decay in $1/k$ and illustrate the Gibbs phenomenon (partial sums at 5, 21, 101 harmonics). *Solution.* $f$ odd and real ⇒ $c_k$ purely imaginary. For $k \neq 0$ even, the integral of $\sin(k\omega_0 t)$ over the two half-periods cancels. For $k$ odd: $c_k = \frac{1}{T_0}\int_0^{T_0}f e^{-ik\omega_0t}dt = \frac{-2i}{T_0}\int_0^{T_0/2}\sin(k\omega_0 t)dt = \frac{-2i}{T_0}\cdot\frac{2\,(1-(-1)^k)}{2k\omega_0} = \frac{-2i}{\pi k}$, that is $\|c_k\| = 2/(\pi\|k\|)$ — consistent with lemma 2.3: the period carries two jumps (of $+2$ at $0$, of $-2$ at $T_0/2$), whose contributions $\frac{2}{2\pi i k}$ and $\frac{-2\,(-1)^k}{2\pi i k}$ add up to $\frac{2(1-(-1)^k)}{2\pi i k} = \frac{-2i}{\pi k}$ for $k$ odd and $0$ for $k$ even. Recombining: $f(t) = \frac{4}{\pi}\sum_{m\geq0}\frac{\sin((2m+1)\omega_0t)}{2m+1}$.
2.  **Numerical Parseval.** Check Parseval's identity on a sampled periodic signal (compare $\sum\|x_n\|^2/N$ and $\sum\|X_k\|^2/N^2$), then explain *why* the DFT preserves the energy up to a factor $N$ (a Vandermonde matrix, unitary up to a factor).
3.  **Quantitative Gibbs (with solution).** Show that for the square wave of exercise 1, the maximum of the partial sum $S_N$ converges to $1 + \frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi \frac{\sin u}{u}du - 1 \approx 1.0895$, i.e. an overshoot of about 9% of the jump. *Solution (sketch).* Near the jump at 0, $S_N f(t) = \frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^{\omega_0 N t}\frac{\sin u}{u}\,du\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}$ (substitution in the Dirichlet kernel $D_N$, prop. 0.2: the partial sum is written $S_Nf(t) = \frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^{N\omega_0t}\mathrm{sinc}$ — oscillations concentrated on a width $O(1/N)$). The maximum of the sinc integral is reached at the first zero of the numerator, $u = \pi$, and equals $\mathrm{Si}(\pi) \approx 1.852$ versus $\mathrm{Si}(\infty) = \pi/2$. The relative overshoot is $\frac{\mathrm{Si}(\pi) - \pi/2}{\pi/2} \approx 17.9\,\%$ of the half-jump, i.e. $\approx 8.95\,\%$ of the full jump — independent of $N$; only the width $\sim 1/N$ shrinks.
4.  **Gaussian (with solution).** Re-prove prop. 3.3 by completing the square: show that $\int e^{-\pi(t + i\nu)^2}dt = \int e^{-\pi t^2}dt = 1$ (move the contour, or differentiate $\int e^{-\pi(t+i\nu)^2}dt$ with respect to $\nu$ and conclude), and deduce the two half-widths (standard deviations) $\sigma_t$, $\sigma_\nu$ and their product. *Solution (key).* $-\pi t^2 - 2\pi i\nu t = -\pi(t+i\nu)^2 - \pi\nu^2$ ⇒ $\hat g = e^{-\pi\nu^2}\cdot\int e^{-\pi u^2}du$ with $u = t + i\nu$ on the horizontal segment — the integral does not depend on $\nu$ (holomorphy + decay at the ends). For $g = e^{-\pi t^2}$: $\sigma_t^2 = 1/(2\pi)$, $\sigma_\nu^2 = 1/(2\pi)$, product $= 1/(4\pi)$: the Gaussian *saturates* Heisenberg-Gabor (th. 3.4).
5.  **Heisenberg (with solution).** Check that equality $\sigma_t\sigma_\nu = 1/(4\pi)$ requires $x' = \lambda t x$ in the proof of th. 3.4, solve this differential equation and conclude that only the Gaussians (translated, modulated, dilated) saturate the inequality. *Solution (key).* Solve $x'(t) = \lambda t\,x(t)$: $x(t) = C e^{\lambda t^2/2}$ with $\lambda < 0$ for integrability; $x \in L^2$ ⇔ $\lambda = -2\pi/\sigma^2$… then a translation in time (center $t_0$) and a modulation (center $\nu_0$), which do not change the standard deviations.
6.  **Aliasing.** Generate a chirp $f(t) = 100 + 400t$ Hz sampled at $f_s = 500$ Hz; compute the spectrogram and interpret the "ghost" trace that goes back down; what apparent frequency does $f = 350$ Hz correspond to? (prop. 4.2: $\|350 - 500\| = 150$ Hz, and the trace rises up to 250 Hz before going back down.)
7.  **Homemade FFT.** Implement the butterfly recursion of th. 5.3 (even/odd recursive function), validate it against `np.fft.fft`, and plot the execution time as a function of $q = \log_2 N$ for $N = 2^q$, $q = 4,\dots,18$; check the $\log$·$N$ slope.
8.  **Convolution via FFT.** Implement the linear convolution via zero-padding + FFT (prop. 5.2), measure the times against `np.convolve` for $n = m = 2^{14}$, and explain the crossing of the complexities.
9.  **Hann filter.** Low-pass FIR design by windowing (example 5.6): ideal response $H(\nu) = \mathbf{1}_{\|\nu\| \leq \nu_c}$, multiplication by a Hann window, inverse transform. Plot the frequency response for $M = 31$ and comment on the transition/aliasing trade-off; compare with Blackman at the same $M$.
10. **Line detection (with solution).** A signal contains $x(t) = \sin(2\pi\cdot50t) + A\sin(2\pi\cdot80t)$ + white noise, with $A = 0.01$ (a line at −40 dB). Show that the raw periodogram does not detect the line at 80 Hz (th. 7.5), then make it emerge with Welch (Hann, segments of 1024). *Solution (key).* Periodogram: leakage of the rectangular window at −13 dB (prop. 5.4) + 100% variance ⇒ the line at −40 dB is drowned. Welch: Hann window (first lobe −31 dB, decay −18 dB/octave) ⇒ the leakage of the 50 Hz line falls below −60 dB; $L \approx 2N/1024$ segments ⇒ the standard deviation of the estimator divided by $\sqrt{L}$: the line at 80 Hz exceeds the detection threshold. Code: `scipy.signal.welch` as in ch. 7.
11. **Mel bank (with solution).** Implement a bank of 26 triangular Mel filters between 0 and $f_s/2$ (formulas of ch. 8), apply it to a spectrogram, then the DCT; check that a vowel and a fricative have very different MFCCs. *Solution (key).* Uniform edges in Mel $m_i = i\,2595\log_{10}(1+f_{max}/700)/26$, converted to Hz by the inverse formula, triangles of normalized area (the highest ones are wider in Hz); energies $E_m = \sum_\nu W_m(\nu)\|S(\nu)\|^2$, log, DCT-II: the vowels (formants, low-Mel energy) concentrate on the first MFCCs, the fricatives (high frequencies) on the following ones.
12. **Project — denoising and spectral loss.** Denoise a recording (white noise added): spectrogram → time-frequency masking (attenuate the cells below an energy threshold) → reconstruction by ISTFT; SNR before/after, musical artifacts. Then compare the *distributions* of original/denoised spectrograms by Gaussian $W_2$ (formula of ch. 8, POT: `ot.gaussian.wass2`) — direct preparation of the M1P2 module.
